You can make the link to be Loaded(item) or Unloaded for example, this would give you nice type level guarantees

Especially if you add item.someLink.try()? to allow shortcuts
I would not recommend it.
Most of the time, SurrealDB needs one database request per HTTP request.
If something is needed, load it, if something is not needed, that field should not even exist on the struct.
Nothing stops you from building a big query that gets all you need all at once
Is there some advantage to this complication?
Avoiding a runtime error at compile-time?)

Why? There is no world that there is one page that lists just the pets (for example "my pets"), and then another page that lists them with owners? (Like current clients that shows all the pets with the owner info)
But if the field doesn't even exist on the struct that the query returns, it's also type-checked at compile time.
You can remove the fils if you add a map at the end
I don't need these when writing in the own query language of SurrealDB.
If you don't do the map/select, it becomes select *
@notramo @Krzysztof Skowronek let's continue here
I think it's possible in Roc to entirely omit the field from the result if it's not loaded. Much simpler than adding a [Loaded, Unloaded].
Also, a query result should be a simple Roc struct, that don't retain any reference to the database.

I think it's not that. Currently fields are loaded with an explicit .fetch(). So the builder object has no way to differentiate between loaded and unloaded

Possibly this API itself needs to be improved

should be a simple Roc struct

It is

By convention, in EF you usually add 2 properties:

  • comment.Post - that's the full object, needs a join
  • comment.PostId - just the foreign key, matched by name convention
So maybe the link could be just either Loaded(entity), or Link(foreign_key)?
Yeah, these are simple struts just wrapped in a tag

But this don't need to be an EF clone. EF is in a different language with a different database.
If you ever tried SurrealDB or EdgeDB in TypeScript, you would understand how much simpler this approach is.
I agree
So you are saying that in surreal when I do equivalent to "select * from pets" it skips the foreign keys/links?

Also, I would not call it an ORM. Most ORMs retain references to the database client, so the object can make lazy queries itself, and this is how waterfall queries sneak in. But with query builders, you build the query once, and get a plain struct that has no database-related code, can not run further queries or anything. It's a simple Roc struct, with the data only, no query builder or anything. If you want further queries, build a new one using the query builder.
I am only saying "in EF it's like this" because in general is pretty good at what it does, and if you want to be inspired by other orm, it should be on the list

notramo said:

Also, I would not call it an ORM. Most ORMs retain references to the database client, so the object can make lazy queries itself, and this is how waterfall queries sneak in. But with query builders, you build the query once, and get a plain struct that has no database-related code, can not run further queries or anything. It's a simple Roc struct, with the data only, no query builder or anything. If you want further queries, build a new one using the query builder.

That's how you use EF Core 99% of the time, without any change tracking is just a query builder and mapper from SQL response to plain dtos

So you are saying that in surreal when I do equivalent to "select * from pets" it skips the foreign keys/links?

Mostly. But there's no concept of "foreign key" in SurrealDB.
Record links are basically queried like if they were embedded in the record, the same syntax as a nested field.
This means it could be possible to derive whether to load the table or not based on field access?

I guess in roc with all the type inference you can do a lot, like it you call fetch(|p| p.owner) just append that property to a type

But then it would be tricky to write a function that takes a pet, because the types would not match, unless you define it in a way that structured matching applies

CREATE person:alice SET
  name = 'Alice',
  friends = [person:bob, person:charlie];

-- traverse with normal field access
SELECT friends.name FROM person:alice;

-- or FETCH
SELECT * FROM person:alice FETCH friends;
There's no JOIN and no "foreign key".

notramo said:

Record links are basically queried like if they were embedded in the record, the same syntax as a nested field.

I've never used surreal specifically, I guess you are able to do something like 'owner.pets.map(|p| p.id)` to get just IDs of pets to put in a message queue or something?
Ok, your example came as I was typing, it makes it much clearer
So a single database trip is multiple statements like above?
Not necessarily.
Or is it just tow way to get the same result?
It is demonstrating two approaches to querying links.
SELECT * is not including links by default, so the FETCH is needed.
But I prefer to select only the fields that I use in that HTTP endpoint.
And that's easy with the automatic join.
Should both ways be available through the ORM?
I would prefer to call it a query builder, not an ORM.
No need to expose these.
Automatically decide under the hood, which is better for the given query.
I need a short way to say what it is :smile:

Here are the feature requests from the previous thread:

  • time series
  • geo
  • database functions
Yep, did not lose them

notramo said:

I would prefer to call it a query builder, not an ORM.

That depends, how do you manage the schema? In EF the c# code is the source of truth, and it generates migrations if you change it, like add a property

You can also generate the code to match existing schema and just not use EF for migrations
The more "decide under the hood" there is, the more of an ORM it becomes, does it not? :slight_smile:
Basically, if * is exposed, the fetch syntax is needed. If not, then it's not needed at all.
It also gives you a command to generate a self contained migration binary you can deploy in a side cart so that only one pod applies the migrations

Another feature that I would like to use:
https://surrealdb.com/docs/reference/query-language/language-primitives/data-types/files

Basically, if * is exposed, the fetch syntax is needed. If not, then it's not needed at all.

If you list out all the fields in the query, then it's not needed.
You can make the final map/select be mandatory, then this discussion done I guess

I'll think about this: since everything is derived from Roc structs, there is not really a place for a * select - at any point all fields are known and listed. I guess this leaves * and FETCH only as escape hatch
Probably yes.
I haven't looked at it yet in detail.
Would it be possible to rebase on the latest changes? LLM agents are quite good at vibe-rebasing nowadays.
I'm working on a big reifier change now, will probably rebase later today. I rebase a few times a week

So do you imagine this being a full orm with roc code being the source of truth, managing migrations, applying then and so on, or would you rather delegate this to surrealkit or something like that and just generate the types from the schema file?
Both solutions can be good.
I just want to try something that works, to evaluate the practicality of this feature in real-world usage.
Not just by checking out the code, but building an actual webapp.
Since surrealdb has live queries, it would great to be able to say '.live()' instead of '.bind()' and get a Stream of responses
And maybe 'live_diff()'
That's one thing I definitely miss from postgres
Oh, I forgot to add live queries to the feature request list.

On the other hand, postgres works very well as a transport for message queues, so you don't need rabbitmq

Tough call :D
We are getting deep into designing a SurrealDB <insert_your_term_here>. @notramo I really hope you will be trying it out extensively, then
One thing I will say about orms, being able to just drop in raw SQL is a great way to cover features you are missing at the time

We are getting deep into designing a SurrealDB <insert_your_term_here>. notramo I really hope you will be trying it out extensively, then

The reason I want these features is that I don't want to try it in demo snippets and example programs, but by building a real, production app for an actual real-world domain.
It may be that you will find cases where the orm approach is not good enough

The example programs always look great, because they are not tied to a real-world domain, and it's easy to only add behavior to the app that can be expressed easily with the current features. The imaginary domain is designed in a way that fits the features of the library. On the other hand, when real-world concepts need to be modeled in code, we can't say "oh, let's not add this feature because our query builder can't express this" or "let's make this behave differently, because it results in simpler code". The behavior needs to be modeled after the real-world behavior, and that's what actually stress-tests these new ideas properly.
I'm glad to know you plan to try it for something concrete
I just want to second that "ORM" is not terminology that makes sense to me in Roc. How do you have an Object-Relational Mapper in a language that does not have Objects? :stuck_out_tongue_wink:
same with DTO

terminology aside, I also have an extremely strongly-held belief that software engineering would have been better if ORMs never existed. I think every single one of them in history, without exception, has been a mistake. I am in general an extremely pro-nuance person, and yet I think ORMs are flat-out bad in the strongest possible terms.
query builders are totally fine though :smile:

To me orm means you can write a query and get objects from it, anything that does auto decoding is an orm

In dotnet people argue whether if a library does only that, maybe it should be called micro-orm
ORM is a mapping between objects and databases
hence the name :wink:
SRM :nerd:
translating from relational rows to objects can be fine, and translating from objects to relational rows can be fine, but the two-way mapping part is where the problems happen

Yeah, maybe the dapper situation rewrote my definition

Why would you say it doesn't make sense for roc? Roc types/struts could be mapped to tables
Most of the queries don't need all of the fields, so it's just wasting RAM and CPU.
deserializing bytes into a Roc value doesn't need a separate name just because it's a database :smile:

a List(U8) coming from a db socket vs a network socket, getting translated from UTF-8 JSON bytes to a record vs serialized postgres bytes to a record...these are not meaningfully different operations, they just have different parsers
The best way for a query builder is to use structural types (anonymous structs) that are derived from the query, and only contain the fields for that given query. Roc has excellent support for these.
"query builder" is just assembling the SQL query to send to the database using a compositional builder style instead of string concatenation and/or interpolation
so query builders are obviously fine, that's just a way to compositionally build up a value that will be serialized into bytes and sent to the db
and serializing/deserializing data to/from a database is no different from doing it over the network, which we do all the time and doesn't need its own name

and all the stuff that ORMs do other than those is what I consider to be a mistake - e.g. the stuff "for ergonomics" that results in N+1 queries, which you normally need to go out of your way to write if you're just using ordinary SQL

In other words, there should be no way to tell whether a struct came from a database query or some other source. The query result should carry zero database client code or query builder code. It should be just the data requested. This is not true with ORMs, because a query result object is also a query builder.

Imo od orm let's you design the database structure exactly how you want, and has a query builder that does things well, is no different than just a query builder

Only difference is that your code cam be the absolute source of truth (unless you do change the database schema not through the orm)

notramo said:

In other words, there should be no way to tell whether a struct came from a database query or some other source. The query result should carry zero database client code or query builder code. It should be just the data requested. This is not true with ORMs, because a query result object is also a query builder.

Why do you think so? That's not axiomatic so to say

In a dotnet context, would you call something like Dapper an ORM? Sometimes I hear people use "ORM" to mean any library that goes in that architectural slot. When the term was first popularized, it came along with a lot more Rails/Java baggage, though.

Dapper has a label of "micro-orm" because it does the decoding from database response to pure dotnet objects, and you give it raw sql, and it used to be like 6x faster than EF Core

Now EF core is as fast and can also take raw sql and mix it with the linq queries
https://sqlkata.com/ this would be a query builder
But this one doesn't know the schema, and tools like Rider (intellij for C#) can't help here, because you don't really see the string until runtime

The "ORM" things that I tend not to like are:

  1. it makes extra queries that the programmer didn't necessarily intend
  2. it hides some SQL functionality I want access to
  3. it expects you to use explicitly mutable-state-OO patterns

I don't know for sure, but I'm guessing others here have similar objections/background to me. I'm not familiar with EF Core. But I'm guessing that a Roc library that had at least some of the features you like about it wouldn't count as an "ORM" to many of us.
That's why I think EF core is amazing, because none of these things are true
But we don't have to model this query builder after EF Core.

1. It doesn't by default, in the old versions they had so called lazy loading, but no one uses that anymore
  2. It exposes pure SQL in both queries and migrations
  3. You can use change tracking and immutability, but you can also write your updates explicitly

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/execute-insert-update-delete#executeupdate

There's also a thing where sometimes people use "object" to mean "non-SQL data structure" and sometimes they use "object" to mean "mutable data structure with app logic methods on it". I think it's useful to have a separate do-nothing type for "this is just a row from the db"
Yeah, but I object to the notion "all orms are bad", and we can make a good one for roc

Yeah, but I object to the notion "all orms are bad", and we can make a good one for roc

Probably that's why I think it's good :)
I think the terminology is irrelevant here. Let's focus on SurrealDB in Roc, as we mostly agree how it should work.

I also hate ORMs with a passion. I had to work with the Django ORM for about a decade building Zulip (the app we're all using now). It was plagued by everything mentioned above.

For most of its history Zulip had a small portion of its database layer written in SQLAlchemy (more of a query builder), and it was glorious. It has handling by far one of the most difficult problems that Zulip solves (complicated search filters) and just silently worked for about a decade. They finally moved that code to Django as well, for the obvious reason they don't want to support both.

I think the terminology is irrelevant here. Let's focus on SurrealDB in Roc, as we mostly agree how it should work.

The [Loaded(item), Unloaded] idea was discarded, because it's against the design principles of this library.

.ExecuteUpdateAsync(setters => setters.SetProperty(b => b.IsVisible, false));

.update(|post| post.is_visible = True)

Maybe something like Surreal.raw("…")? But then we lose type checking. The string could contain a syntax error.

in Roc it would be something like

ontext.Blogs
    .filter(|b| b.rating < 3)
    .execute_update(setters => setters.set_property(|b|  b.is_visible, Bool.False))

and this is a single database trip doing update blogs set isVisible = false where rating < 3
you get the column names from lambdas |b| b.is_visible with this reification
everything is fully typed of course

not necessarly, if you know the schema you can parse the raw SQL, right?
Comptime parsing?

.update(|post| {
  post.is_visible = True
})

(edit: this is also invalid, because post is immutable)

so = is not a valid syntax, right?

the purpose of setters is so that reification can parse this and say user want to set b.is_visible to False

so blogs.filter(|p| p.id == 5).update(|p| {..p, soft_delete : Bool.True}) or whatever the syntax is
that code would never run, so you can do whatever you want actually :)

what's better, you can do stuff like

blogs.filter(|p| p.id == 5).update(|p| {..p, body: new_body, body_lenght: new_body.len()}) -- all that would happen in the db

that's the reification - you get a syntax tree that says update got passed a lambda that updates field "active" to a value of "not field acive" then you have the query builder looks at that and outputs update blog set active = not active where id = 5
that's the magic bit
(flashbang warning) https://dev.to/turalsuleymani/solid-introduction-to-expression-trees-in-c-1c4i
btw, in F# (the functional language for dotnet) there is a shorthand lambda syntax, so |x| x.SomeProperty can be written as just _.SomeProperty - quite usefull for cases like this

you would need to parse the passed string at compile time

if it can't be parsed then, you have add the type annotation to the result

then just type the output with annotation or let it get inferred
and fails just like you would Json.from_str

I think it should be even fine to do things like

latest_blogs: Query(Blog)
latest_blogs = db.query_raw("you fancy sql") # query is lazy in this example

latest_blogs.filter(|b| b.title.len() > 10).bind()

so you would end up with

with latest_blogs as ( your_fancy_sql) select * from latest_blogs where length(title) > 10)

because like you said then you have to maintain the whole parser up to date

plus, comptime parsing would help you with something more dynamic, like if request.show_archived ... and you have to add a where clause at runtime conditionally
that's where the query builder comes in

because you can esily do 

$query = db.blogs

if request.hide_archived {
    $query = $query.filter(|b| !b.is_archived)
}

if request.filter = Some(filter) {
     $query = $query.filter(|b| b.title.contains(filter) || b.body.contains(filter))
}

It's possible with comptime SurrealQL parsing too: write one query as a static Str with no dynamic interpolation or concatenation, and pass hide_archived as an argument, and add the if inside SurrealQL.
yeah, sure, but that SQL would get HUGE
Not that much. SurrealQL is more concise than SQL.
at previous job we a request with like 100 different parameters :) the function to build the query was couple hundred lines

You glance over the code when you need the semantics. When you wonder where could be performance issues, without profiling first, you pay attention to details like what is the execution context of some pure code - is it Roc compiled binary, or is it database filter expression.

The code does not need a 100-word essay prefacing every change of execution context - if you are trying to debug logic or performance you should know what you are working with, and whether you are using a query builder that translates your code to DB commands, without red flag emojis highlighting the code.

What's the problem with Tcp?

The issue is with basic-webserver's design.
Claude:

  1. Every read gives up after 30 seconds. The limit is hard-coded (src/tcp.rs:22). On a quiet live query, the read fails with TimedOut and the app has to reconnect. Bytes from a partly finished read may be lost; the subagent inferred this rather than verified it.
  2. Waiting for data ties up a worker. A read holds one of the 32 Roc worker slots until bytes arrive (src/tcp.rs:357-386, Sleep.roc:3-6). Waiting for pushed messages inside a request handler uses up a slot for as long as it waits.
  3. Nothing runs unless a request comes in. The app's only entry points are init!, respond! and shutdown! (main.roc:11-15). No background loop can keep reading the socket between requests.
  4. Only one user of the connection at a time. A second read or write on the same stream returns StreamBusy (src/tcp.rs:362-380). A handler parked on a read would block every other handler that wants to send an RPC.
  5. App state cannot change. Context is read-only startup data (design.md:144). There is nowhere to keep half-received frames, the table of pending request ids, or the state of live subscriptions.
I work on a cloudflare workers platform that supports websocket, but you need to want to design your app around the workers' limitations
